editorial.headline: Wholesale Textiles: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale trade in textiles, batik cloth and household linen is nationally open to full foreign ownership—but Bali blocks PMA registration under its permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity cannot be registered in Bali by a foreign investor today. That is the decisive local fact about this wholesale textile activity, even though the national record marks it TERBUKA and allows foreign ownership up to 100%. The scope is focused on wholesale trade in products of the textile industry: assorted textiles and fabrics, batik cloth, and household linen—fabrics intended for domestic use. Those examples keep the activity grounded in the merchandise itself. It is wholesale trade in the textile goods expressly named in the record, from general fabric to batik and linen for household needs. National openness matters, but it is only one part of the practical reading.

The classification is available at every scale listed in the record: Micro, Small, Medium, and Large. That broad availability makes it relevant to businesses of different sizes, while leaving the activity’s subject unchanged: textiles, fabrics, batik cloth, and household linen in wholesale trade. At national level, its PMA status is TERBUKA and its maximum foreign ownership is 100%, with Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 identified as the source. In practical terms, the national ceiling permits a fully foreign-owned PMA for this activity. The key question is therefore not whether national policy admits foreign ownership, but whether the province where registration is sought changes the result.

Bali does change it. Its local status is blocked on risk-class grounds. The stated reason is precise: at the Large scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low on every scope, and Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. For this activity, the cited moratorium dates to May 2026. The result should be stated without euphemism: for a foreign investor, this activity cannot be registered in Bali today. That does not reduce or rewrite the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling; it prevents Bali registration for PMA under the province’s stated risk-based rule.

The national and Bali positions answer different parts of the registration question. Nationally, the activity is open to PMA and can be fully foreign owned. In Bali, it is unavailable to PMA registration because its applicable risk classification falls within the permanent moratorium. That local block is the operative conclusion for a PMA considering this activity in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, the activity is open to PMA and can be fully foreign owned.
